transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello Mrs. Al-Rashid. It is good to see you again.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Hello Doctor.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I wanted to come back and talk with you today because I know we left several of your questions unanswered during our last visit.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I have been thinking about it a lot. I cannot quite understand how this happens in a hospital.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see that you are still very shaken by this. It is an incredibly heavy thing to process, and I want us to take as much time as we need today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just... I trust the doctors. I always do. To find out there was a mistake... it is very distressing.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I recognize how unsettling it is, especially when you have placed your trust in us to keep you safe.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So, what exactly happened? You said it was about my weight.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, I want to be very clear about that. The chemotherapy dose was calculated using your weight from three months ago. Because you have lost a significant amount of weight during your treatment, the dose you received was higher than what your current weight required.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Because I am thinner now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Exactly. The medication is measured by how much a person weighs. Since we used the old, higher weight, you received too much of the drug. Does that explanation make sense to you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, I think I understand. But why was the old weight used?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a failure in our process. The previous weight was still listed in the chart, and it was not updated before the dose was ordered.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And you were the one who gave it to me?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I was. I am so sorry that this happened. We failed to double-check the current weight, and I take full responsibility for that mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I do not know what to say. I just wanted to get better.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can hear how disappointing and frightening this feels. You came here to heal, and instead, you have to deal with the stress of a medical error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel very small in this. I just do the things you tell me to do.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you have been a wonderful patient, following every instruction. Which makes it even more frustrating that we did not do our part correctly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Will this make me sicker? Will the overdose hurt my organs?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is the most important question. We have been monitoring your blood work closely. While the dose was higher than intended, your kidney and liver functions are still within a safe range.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Based on the tests from yesterday, yes. But I want to make sure I have explained the situation clearly. Do you feel you have a good understanding now of why the dose was wrong?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I think so. It was the wrong weight.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So, what happens now? How do we fix this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are going to keep a very close eye on your blood markers.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When will I know if I am okay?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will just keep checking the labs.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But what about the next dose? Do I take it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will look at the schedule. I think we will just see how you feel over the next few days.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Do I need to do anything? Should I be watching for certain signs at home?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You can just let us know if you feel different.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't know what "different" means, Doctor. Should I be worried about my breathing or my stomach?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will figure that out. We'll probably send some updates.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm not entirely sure on the timing yet, but we will keep you posted.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel very uneasy. I do not know if I can trust the next bottle of medicine.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can feel the doubt in your voice. It is completely natural to feel that way after what happened. Your trust was broken, and I know that is not something that is fixed overnight.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to know that it will not happen again.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. That is the most important thing for you right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes. How do I know the next dose is right?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will be monitoring you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is not a plan, Doctor.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. We'll just take it one step at a time.

H.justification: Resident allows the patient to finish all turns, maintains a regulated pace during pushback, and uses no rushing language.

E.justification: The error (overdose due to old weight) is named explicitly by the second resident turn, uses lay language, and comprehension is checked twice (01:32 and 03:08).

A.justification: Resident uses direct apology language ('I am so sorry'), takes full personal responsibility ('I take full responsibility'), and maintains this without deflection.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('shaken', 'unsettling', 'disappointing and frightening', 'doubt') and references the patient's specific experience of trust.

T.justification: The resident provides only placeholders and vague responses ('we will figure that out', 'we'll just take it one step at a time') with no timelines, patient role, or prevention plan.
